content.title: About
content.content: Creamsicle is a creamy‑orange frozen treat on a stick, popular in the United States since the early 1970s. It features a bright orange color, a smooth creamy flavor with orange notes, and a crunchy chocolate coating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Creamsicle was introduced by Popsicle in 1971.
The name combines “cream” and the suffix “sicle” (from “popsicle”).
The original recipe used natural orange essence and real cream.
Creamsicles are often associated with summer camps and school recesses.
In some countries there are fruit‑flavored variants, but the classic remains the most popular.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The creamy portion provides a modest amount of calcium, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Vitamin C from orange
items.content: The orange flavor contributes a small dose of vitamin C, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Sugar and fat deliver fast‑acting energy, useful during active play.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Creamsicles contain a considerable amount of sugar, so they should be eaten in moderation, especially by people with diabetes.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The creamy component may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Cold treat
items.content: Because of its low temperature, the treat can cause “brain freeze” or tooth sensitivity if consumed too quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Creamsicles are typically eaten straight from the wrapper, allowing the frozen core to melt in the mouth. They can be stored in the freezer for up to 6 months. For a softer texture, let them sit at room temperature for a few minutes before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep Creamsicles in the freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once removed from the packaging, avoid refreezing to maintain texture quality.

fish-noodles-and-vegetables-excluding-ca.title: Fish, noodles, and vegetables without carrots, broccoli, and dark-green leafy; cheese sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of boiled or pan‑fried fish, egg or wheat noodles, and a mix of vegetables (such as bell pepper, zucchini, peas), deliberately excluding carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens. All components are coated with a smooth cheese sauce made from milk, cheese and seasonings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Combining fish and cheese is a classic feature of Mediterranean cuisine.
Noodles readily absorb the flavor of the sauce, making the dish more robust.
Leaving out carrots and broccoli makes the meal lighter for sensitive stomachs.
Cheese sauce is often prepared with processed cheese, which melts easily and gives a velvety texture.
Variations may replace fish with seafood such as shrimp.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fatty fish like salmon or mackerel contain omega‑3s that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Noodles and vegetables supply B1, B2 and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce adds calcium, beneficial for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: The dish contains no added sugars, making it suitable for blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Fish or dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to fish or dairy may experience adverse reactions.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese sauces often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Possible contaminants in fish
items.content: Some fish species may contain mercury; choose young or low‑mercury varieties.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese sauce made from milk can cause discomfort for those with lactose intolerance.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, drizzling the cheese sauce over the fish and noodles just before serving. Garnish with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill for extra aroma. Optionally sprinkle grated Parmesan or add a lemon wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Store the cheese sauce separately and reheat before use to prevent fat separation.

pizza-with-meat-other-than-pepperoni-fro.title: Pizza with meat (not pepperoni), school lunch, thick crust

content.title: About
content.content: A meat pizza that differs from classic pepperoni is often served in school cafeterias as a hearty lunch. The dough has a thick crust (3417), making it denser and more filling. The meat topping can be beef, chicken, or ham, combined with tomato sauce, cheese, and vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A thick crust retains more moisture, keeping the toppings juicy.
In school menus pizza is considered a source of protein and carbohydrates for active children.
Meat used in school pizzas undergoes strict quality and sanitary checks.
Pizza is typically prepared in large batches in schools, ensuring consistent taste and texture.
A "chicken and vegetable pizza" variant is often offered as a lower‑calorie option.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat provides a complete set of amino acids essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium, supporting bone and tooth health in children.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and meat contain vitamins B6 and B12, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Dietary fiber from vegetables
items.content: Added vegetables (bell pepper, onion) increase fiber content, aiding digestion.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: The combination of carbs from the crust and protein from the meat provides sustained satiety.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Thick crust and cheese make the pizza calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially for less active children.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt in the sauce and cheese can raise sodium intake, which is undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Cheese and certain meats may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: If margarine is used instead of olive oil, trans fats may be present.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the pizza into serving pieces and eat it while hot. Fresh vegetables or herbs can be added for extra nutrition. For a crisp crust, reheat briefly in an oven or grill rather than a microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore crust crispness. Discard if it develops an off‑smell or taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Venison is lean deer meat rich in protein, iron and B‑vitamins. Paired with a savory gravy made from broth, onions and spices, the dish becomes tender, juicy and full‑flavored.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is considered a more diet‑friendly meat than beef because of its low fat content.
In the wild, deer feed on grasses, leaves and berries, which gives the meat a “wild” character.
Traditional venison dishes come from northern Europe and North America.
Gravy is often enriched with red wine or berry reductions to highlight the natural taste of the meat.
Venison can be used in dishes ranging from simple stews to sophisticated fusion recipes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Venison provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with beef, venison contains less saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: High iron content
items.content: The iron in venison is highly bioavailable and helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B12 and B6 support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals and antioxidants
items.content: Venison supplies zinc, selenium and coenzyme Q10, which aid immune health and cellular protection.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to game meat, such as rash or swelling.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Wild venison can harbor parasites; it should be cooked to an internal temperature of 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: High purine content
items.content: People with gout or elevated uric acid should limit venison consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot venison with gravy, typically alongside mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce or boiled vegetables. The meat can be sliced thin, quickly seared, and then drenched with the prepared gravy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh venison in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. Frozen venison can be stored up to 6 months at –18 °C in an airtight bag.
